title: Nineveh Falls and No One Mourns
overview: Nahum pictures the coming fall of Nineveh, capital of the brutal Assyrian empire, and says the nations it crushed will cheer when it goes.

parts.label: The city of blood (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Nineveh is charged with endless killing, lies and plunder, and the poem then plunges the reader into the chaos of its final battle, with bodies piled in the streets. The picture of a seductive prostitute and sorceress most likely stands for how Assyria lured smaller nations with trade and alliances, then trapped them as subjects.

parts.label: Stripped and shamed (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: The LORD declares himself against Nineveh using a harsh, degrading image of a woman stripped and pelted with filth, drawn from how women could be publicly shamed in that world. It stands for the proud city being exposed and humiliated, with no one left who cares enough to mourn.

parts.label: Remember Thebes (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: Thebes, Egypt's great city on the Nile, was ringed by water and backed by allies from Nubia (called Cush), Put and Libya, yet Assyria itself captured it around 663 BC with terrible atrocities. Nahum's point is that Nineveh is no safer and will soon be the one staggering like a drunk and looking for somewhere to hide.

parts.label: Defenses that will not hold (vv. 12-15a)
parts.note: Nineveh's forts will drop like ripe figs shaken into a waiting mouth, and the call to store water and make bricks for the siege is mockery, since fire and sword will come anyway. Nineveh did fall in 612 BC to the Babylonians and Medes, and digs at the site show signs of burning.

parts.label: Locusts that fly away (vv. 15b-17)
parts.note: Assyria's merchants and officials are as many as locusts, but like locusts warming on a wall they vanish once the day heats up. The image seems to say that the people who grew rich from the empire will desert it when trouble comes.

parts.label: A wound that will not heal (vv. 18-19)
parts.note: Assyria's leaders, called shepherds, lie asleep, probably meaning dead, and the people scatter like sheep with no one to gather them. Everyone who hears the news claps, because every nation around had suffered Assyria's cruelty.

think: When a cruel power finally falls, is the relief people feel a form of justice, or something more complicated than that?
